passage: At a beach near Melbourne, Bao and Dalia dug a moat around their sandcastle. "The waves keep filling it with sand!" Dalia groaned. Bao thought. "You dig, I'll make a wall." Dalia scooped while Bao patted wet sand into a bank. When a small wave slid in, the water filled the moat but stopped at the wall. They grabbed each other's hands and jumped. "We did it!" Then they made the wall taller, together.

qa.q: What did Bao make while Dalia dug?
qa.a: Bao patted wet sand into a bank to make a wall.

qa.q: How do Bao and Dalia feel when the wave stops at the wall?
qa.a: They feel proud and joyful, shown by grabbing hands, jumping and shouting "We did it!"

qa.q: Which choice made their plan work?
qa.a: Splitting the jobs, one digging and one building the wall, let them protect the moat faster than either could alone.

qa.q: What would change if Dalia had kept digging alone?
qa.a: The waves would likely keep filling the moat, and Dalia might give up frustrated without Bao's wall.

grounding: Two children divide tasks to build a sand wall that protects their shared moat.

passage: In the anganwadi, Zainab and Ganga wanted the wooden train track to reach all the way to the door. "Not enough straight pieces," Ganga said. Zainab found curved ones in the basket. "Put two curves, it goes the same way." Ganga held the track steady while Zainab clicked pieces in. When the didi called lunch, the track stopped one step short. They asked to leave it, and after lunch they finished it, cheering as the engine rolled through.

qa.q: Where did the children want the train track to reach?
qa.a: They wanted it to reach all the way to the door.

qa.q: What might Ganga have been worried about when saying there were not enough pieces?
qa.a: Ganga may have feared they could not finish the track and reach the door.

qa.q: What went well in how they handled lunch interrupting?
qa.a: They asked to leave the track standing and came back after lunch to finish it.

qa.q: How might the anganwadi didi see their project?
qa.a: She may be impressed that two small children kept a shared goal through a break and worked it out together. 😊

grounding: Two children at a centre work together to build a train track that reaches the door.

passage: My cousin Wasim is five. On Sunday I watched him and his friend from next door try to build a block tower as high as the window. Wasim held the bottom steady with both hands. His friend stood on a stool and placed blocks. "Slowly, slowly," Wasim said. When it wobbled, they stopped and agreed to use the big blocks first. It reached the window. They both yelled for me to look. — Pankaj

qa.q: How high did the boys want their block tower to be?
qa.a: They wanted it as high as the window.

qa.q: What does "Slowly, slowly" suggest Wasim was feeling?
qa.a: He was probably careful and a bit nervous that the tower would fall, though Pankaj can only guess from his words.

qa.q: What could an adult do to help such teamwork continue?
qa.a: Stay nearby, keep the stool safe, and praise how they agreed to change plans when the tower wobbled.

qa.q: Why do you think the boys wanted Pankaj to look?
qa.a: They wanted someone to see and share their success, showing how proud they were of what they made together.

grounding: An older cousin watches two boys cooperate and change their plan to build a tall block tower.

passage:
Monday: Madhuri and Elizabeth both wanted to put the top block on their tower. They pulled, and it crashed.
Wednesday: Elizabeth said, 'You hold the bottom, I'll add.' It wobbled at ten blocks, and Madhuri steadied it with both hands.
Friday: they took turns, one block each, counting aloud. When it reached the window ledge, they jumped and hugged, and asked the teacher to take a photo.

qa.q: How high did the tower reach on Friday?
qa.a: It reached the window ledge.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri and Elizabeth jump and hug on Friday?
qa.a: They felt proud and happy because they had reached their goal together by taking turns.

qa.q: What changed between Monday and Friday that made it work?
qa.a: They moved from both grabbing to dividing jobs and taking turns, which let them work as a team toward one outcome.

qa.q: How might the teacher see the children's progress over the week?
qa.a: The teacher would likely see real growth in their teamwork and be glad to take the photo.

grounding: Illustrates children learning to collaborate toward a shared outcome across several days.

passage: The rain was stopping, and the puddle by the gate was shrinking fast. 'Quick, Lalremsiami, the dam!' Siddharth scooped mud while she pressed it into a wall. 'You bring stones, I'll pack,' she said. Water trickled through a gap. 'Plug it!' He shoved in a leaf. Their paper boat rocked in the little pond they had saved. The sun came out, and they cheered, muddy to the elbows.

qa.q: What did Siddharth use to plug the gap?
qa.a: He shoved in a leaf.

qa.q: What were the children worried about as the rain stopped?
qa.a: They were worried the puddle would shrink before their dam held water for the paper boat.

qa.q: What helped them succeed under time pressure?
qa.a: Lalremsiami split the jobs, stones for Siddharth and packing for her, so they worked quickly toward one goal.

qa.q: How might a parent seeing them muddy to the elbows react?
qa.a: They might groan about the mess but also smile at how well the two worked together.

grounding: Shows two children collaborating on a shared building goal against a time constraint.

passage: In the courtyard of their Pune housing colony, Ojas and Salma, both five, had one goal: a sand tower tall enough to reach the bottom of the slide. "You bring water, I pat," Salma said. Ojas ran back and forth with a cup. When one side slumped, they both stopped. "More water," Ojas said. "No, too much," said Salma. "Less!" They patted together, carefully. The tower touched the slide, and they jumped up and down, shouting.

qa.q: What was the tower supposed to reach?
qa.a: The bottom of the slide.

qa.q: What were Ojas and Salma feeling when the tower touched the slide?
qa.a: They were thrilled and proud of reaching their goal together.

qa.q: What helped them work as a team?
qa.a: Splitting the jobs, water and patting, and talking about what went wrong when one side slumped.

qa.q: How might Salma see Ojas as a partner?
qa.a: As someone who followed the plan and stayed to fix the problem, which made the tower possible.

grounding: Shows two young children working together towards one goal, a tall sand tower.

passage:
"We need a train long enough for all the animals," said Uday.
"Twelve boxes," said his brother Anirban, counting. "We only have eight."
"Ask Amma for the shoe boxes!"
"You tape, I'll push them together."
"Your tape is crooked."
"Then you tape and I'll hold."
Uday held; Anirban taped.
"Elephant goes in the last box, he's heavy."
"Last box. Okay."
When the train was done, they lined up every animal and pulled it round the room together, both hands on the string.

qa.q: How many boxes did they say they needed?
qa.a: Twelve boxes.

qa.q: How did Uday feel when Anirban said his tape was crooked?
qa.a: He may have felt a little stung, but he stayed calm and willing, swapping jobs so the train could get finished.

qa.q: Which choice kept the building going, and why?
qa.a: Swapping roles when the tape went crooked, because it fixed the problem without a fight.

qa.q: What would change if one brother had insisted on doing everything alone?
qa.a: The train would take longer, and they would lose the fun of building it together.

grounding: Shows two young brothers planning and building a toy train together to fit all their animals.

passage:
Nursery note from Rukmini, Thursday
Charu (5) and two friends decided to build a bridge of blocks so the toy cars could cross the "river" (a blue cloth). Charu held the two ends steady with her hands while the others laid the long block across. It fell twice. The third time, Charu said, "Let's make the towers fatter," and they did. The bridge held. They cheered and drove every car across. I took a photo for the wall and asked them to explain it at circle time.

qa.q: What did the blue cloth stand for?
qa.a: The "river".

qa.q: What might Charu have felt when the bridge held on the third try?
qa.a: Probably proud and excited, since her idea of fatter towers worked.

qa.q: Why is asking them to explain it at circle time a good idea?
qa.a: It lets them put their teamwork into words and feel their shared effort was noticed.

qa.q: How might Charu's two friends see her part in the building?
qa.a: They might see her as the one with the good idea, while they did the placing, so the success felt shared.

grounding: Shows young children cooperating on a block bridge and solving a problem together, noted by their teacher.

passage: After school in their village near Kolhapur, Tushar and Shankar, both six, decided to stop the little stream behind the temple. "You bring stones, I'll bring mud," Tushar said. Shankar carried stones in his shirt. Tushar packed mud between them. The water leaked through. "More mud here!" Shankar pointed. They pressed together, four hands, until the water rose into a small pool. "We did it!" They splashed in their dam until Tushar's Aai called them for dinner.

qa.q: Where was the little stream?
qa.a: Behind the temple.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel when the water rose into a pool?
qa.a: Tushar felt excited and proud of what they built together.

qa.q: What helped their teamwork succeed?
qa.a: Dividing the jobs, stones and mud, and fixing the leak together when Shankar pointed it out.

qa.q: How might Tushar's Aai see the two muddy boys?
qa.a: Aai probably feels amused and maybe a little exasperated, but glad they played so well together.

grounding: Two village six-year-olds work together to dam a stream, dividing jobs and fixing a leak.

passage: During snow festival week in Sapporo, Yuki and Rania, both five, decided to build a snowman taller than Yuki's father. "You roll the bottom, I roll the middle," Rania said. Their snowballs grew lumpy and huge. The middle one was too heavy to lift. Yuki pushed from one side; Rania pulled from the other. It rolled up on top, crooked. "The head is my job!" Yuki said. They argued about the nose, then used a carrot and a mitten. Their snowman leaned, but it stood.

qa.q: What did they use for the snowman's nose?
qa.a: A carrot and a mitten.

qa.q: What might Rania have felt when the middle ball was too heavy?
qa.a: Rania probably felt frustrated, then relieved when pushing and pulling together worked.

qa.q: How did the children reach their goal together?
qa.a: They divided the jobs, pushed and pulled together on the heavy ball, and found a compromise for the nose.

qa.q: How might Yuki's father see the leaning snowman?
qa.a: He would probably feel amused and proud that they built it together, even crooked.

grounding: During a Japanese snow festival, two five-year-olds collaborate to build a tall snowman.

passage: In the week before Diwali, the kindergarten teacher gave each table one giant paper lantern to finish. Hafsa and Gurpreet, both six, looked at the flat sheet. "You fold, I stick," Gurpreet said. Hafsa folded the pleats; Gurpreet dabbed glue. It kept springing open. "Hold it! Hold it!" Hafsa squeezed while Gurpreet counted to ten. It stayed. They added a tail of shiny strips, arguing over colours until they chose one each. When the teacher hung it up, they stood underneath, grinning at each other.

qa.q: What did each table get to finish?
qa.a: One giant paper lantern.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling standing under the lantern?
qa.a: Hafsa felt proud and happy, grinning at what they had made together.

qa.q: How did they solve the problem of the lantern springing open?
qa.a: Hafsa held it while Gurpreet counted to ten, working together until the glue set.

qa.q: How might the teacher see their lantern?
qa.a: The teacher probably felt pleased, seeing them cooperate on one shared goal.

grounding: Before Diwali in kindergarten, two six-year-olds cooperate to finish a paper lantern.

passage:
I'm Dolma from the next building. On a hot summer evening I saw Disha and three other children building a sandcastle in the colony sandpit.

At first each dug separately. Then Disha said, "Let's make one big castle." One carried water, one patted walls, one made a moat with a stick. Disha pressed a leaf on top as a flag.

They cheered when it stood. I don't know who had the idea first, but they all seemed proud.

qa.q: What did Disha press on top of the castle?
qa.a: Disha pressed a leaf on top as a flag.

qa.q: How did the children seem to feel when the castle stood?
qa.a: They seemed proud and happy, cheering together.

qa.q: How could adults encourage this kind of teamwork?
qa.a: Give them space and materials, and praise how they shared jobs to build one castle.

qa.q: How does Dolma see the children's play?
qa.a: Dolma watches with interest and enjoyment, noticing their teamwork though unsure who led it.

grounding: A neighbour observes children working together to build one sandcastle on a summer evening.

passage:
First day of winter holidays: Shankar and Wasim each build their own block tower. Both fall.

Next day: they build together but argue over which block goes next. The tower falls, and Wasim cries.

Christmas Eve: Shankar says, "You hold, I'll put." Wasim holds the bottom steady while Shankar adds blocks. The tower grows taller than Wasim. They shout for everyone to come and see.

qa.q: How tall did the tower grow on Christmas Eve?
qa.a: The tower grew taller than Wasim.

qa.q: How did Shankar and Wasim feel when the tower stood on Christmas Eve?
qa.a: They were proud and excited, shouting for everyone to come and see.

qa.q: What helped them build the tower together?
qa.a: Taking different jobs, one holding and one placing, helped them work toward the same goal.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel after the arguments on the second day?
qa.a: Wasim felt upset and frustrated, crying when the tower fell.

grounding: Over the winter holidays, two children learn to work together to build a tall block tower.

passage:
The monsoon rain was stopping, and the gutter stream outside the Kochi house would soon dry up. Kavitha and Suraj had only a few minutes.

"Quick! You fold, I'll write names," Kavitha said.

Suraj folded paper boats as fast as he could. Kavitha wrote a name on each one. They raced out together and launched six boats in a line.

The last boat sailed just as the stream slowed. They jumped and hugged.

qa.q: How many boats did they launch?
qa.a: They launched six boats in a line.

qa.q: How did Kavitha and Suraj feel when the last boat sailed?
qa.a: They were excited and happy, jumping and hugging.

qa.q: What helped them finish the boats in time?
qa.a: Dividing the jobs, one folding and one writing names, helped them work quickly toward the same goal.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel folding boats so fast?
qa.a: Suraj might feel rushed but determined to finish before the rain stopped.

grounding: As the monsoon rain stops, two children work together under time pressure to launch a fleet of paper boats.

passage: During Ganesh Chaturthi every lane of the Nagpur colony had a pandal, so Omkar and Sangeeta decided to build their own from wooden blocks. "You do the walls, I'll do the roof," Sangeeta said. Omkar lined up the long blocks; Sangeeta balanced flat ones on top. When one wall wobbled, Omkar held it steady while she slid a block behind it. "Now it's strong!" The roof reached Omkar's chin. They set a tiny clay Ganpati inside and ran to fetch Ajji.

qa.q: Who built the walls and who built the roof?
qa.a: Omkar lined up the walls and Sangeeta balanced the roof on top.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when she said "Now it's strong!"?
qa.a: She felt proud and relieved that their teamwork had fixed the wobbling wall. 😊

qa.q: What made their teamwork work?
qa.a: They split the jobs clearly and helped each other when a problem came up, like holding the wall steady.

qa.q: What might Ajji think when she sees the pandal?
qa.a: Ajji would likely feel proud and touched that the two children planned and built it together.

grounding: Illustrates young children working together toward one goal, building a festival pandal from blocks.
